query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The differences in mechanical properties among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets are governed by how each alloy responds to thermomechanical processing, specifically through the degree of grain refinement and any secondary nanoscale precipitate formation. These microstructural changes modify dislocation–grain boundary interactions, thus altering strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary derivatives in their as-cast or homogenized single-phase FCC state.
generation.intervention: Apply a standardized thermomechanical processing protocol (e.g., rolling followed by controlled recrystallization annealing) aimed at inducing grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Processing performed under controlled deformation rates and annealing temperatures at room temperature; all alloys must initially have single-phase FCC microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size distribution (i.e., increased grain boundary density) and the possible occurrence of nanoscale, incoherent precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement enhances strength via the Hall–Petch mechanism by increasing dislocation obstacles, while variations in alloy composition may lead to differential secondary phase (precipitate) formation. This interplay can strengthen the material but may also compromise ductility in some subsets.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys that achieve finer grain sizes with minimal precipitate formation will display increased yield strength with maintained ductility, whereas alloys with more precipitate formation may show comparable or slightly higher strength at the expense of ductility.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility) of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed under standard thermomechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys processed under controlled TMP conditions. It may not hold for alloys that develop multiphase microstructures or are processed outside the specific deformation/annealing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in property enhancements among the subsets remain uncertain due to potential variations in precipitate formation kinetics and grain growth behaviors that are sensitive to small compositional changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, quaternary, and ternary subsets with initially single-phase FCC microstructures. Subject all samples to an identical thermomechanical processing protocol (rolling and controlled recrystallization annealing). Characterize the resulting grain size distributions and check for the presence of nanoscale precipitates using EBSD and TEM. Conduct room temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: Grain size distribution via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
Secondary phase or precipitate identification and quantification via transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Stress-strain curves from room temperature tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after identical TMP, variations in mechanical properties (strength and ductility) among the alloys do not correlate with differences in grain refinement or precipitate formation, or if all alloy subsets show nearly identical microstructures and properties irrespective of composition, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe potential of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to exhibit an extraordinary combination of properties by shifting the compositional regime from the corners towards the centers of phase diagrams has led to worldwide attention by material scientists. Here we present a strong and ductile non-equiatomic HEA obtained after friction stir processing (FSP). A transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) assisted HEA with composition Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at.%) was severely deformed by FSP and evaluated for its microstructure-mechanical property relationship. The FSP-engineered microstructure of the TRIP HEA exhibited a substantially smaller grain size, and optimized fractions of face-centered cubic (f.c.c., γ) and hexagonal close-packed (h.c.p., ε) phases, as compared to the as-homogenized reference material. This results in synergistic strengthening via TRIP, grain boundary strengthening, and effective strain partitioning between the γ and ε phases during deformation, thus leading to enhanced strength and ductility of the TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA engineered via FSP.

It is well known that grain refinement is an effective way to improve the mechanical properties with a combination of high strength and good ductility. Previous studies have shown that the grain size of HEAs can be controlled by rolling and recrystallization [,,,]. The ternary/quaternary derivatives of the FeCoNiCrMn HEA with no Mn included have also been systematically studied to determine their phase stabilities, microstructure, and microhardness evolution []. However, the factors that affect the grain growth behavior of HEAs and the corresponding activation energies of grain growth kinetics have not been fully clarified, although they are crucial for designing alloys for future engineering applications. In this study, the grain growth behavior and Hall–Petch relationship exhibited by FeCoNiCrPd HEA, FeCoNiCrMn HEA, and their ternary/quaternary derivatives with the Mn included were studied and compared with the traditional alloys. The factors affecting the grain growth characteristics and the grain refinement hardening revealed in these high/medium entropy alloys (H/MEAs) are also discussed.

However, the mechanical properties have only been reported for as-recrystallized Co-rich HEAs. The microstructure has a strong correlation with the mechanical properties of metals and alloys, which are usually tuned by thermomechanical processing (TMP), such as rolling, compression, and torsion, combined with heat-treatment [,,,,,,,,,]. The influence of TMP on the resultant microstructure and the correlation between the microstructure and mechanical performance of the newly developed Co-rich HEAs have not yet been revealed. The regulation of the microstructure is a prerequisite for optimizing the mechanical performance of metals and alloys; thus, gaining a deep understanding of microstructure optimization and its influence on their mechanical properties is crucial. These will become guidelines for fabricating high-performance materials that deserve in-depth investigation. In this study, we aimed to clarify the effect of TMP on the microstructure and room-temperature tensile properties of Co-rich Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) TRIP-HEA.
